title: 1.1 Bronchial Asthma
content:
BRONCHIAL ASTHMA

A reversible, chronic inflammatory airway disease with bronchial hyper-responsiveness.

title: 1.1.1 Definition and Classification
content:
DEFINITION AND CLASSIFICATION


DEFINITION

A reversible chronic inflammatory airway disease characterized by bronchial hyper-responsiveness of the airways to various stimuli, leading to widespread bronchoconstriction, airflow limitation and inflammation of the bronchi, causing symptoms of cough, wheeze, chest tightness and dyspnea.

 * Clinically: recurrent episodes of wheezing, breathlessness, chest tightness, and cough, particularly at night / early morning.
 * Physiologically: widespread, reversible narrowing of the bronchial airways and a marked increase in bronchial responsiveness.


PREVALENCE

 * Prevalence of asthma is increasing in many countries, together with allergy.
 * It is particularly seen in children and young adults, where it may affect up to 15% of the population.
 * It shows geographical variation: commoner in more developed countries.


CLASSIFICATION

Atopic (extrinsic / allergic) Non-atopic (intrinsic / non-allergic) Frequency
~70% ~30% Mechanism IgE-mediated immune response to environmental antigens
Triggered by non-immune stimuli Skin-prick test
Positive to common inhalant allergens (dust mite, animal dander, pollens, fungi)
Negative Serum IgE Raised in atopic individuals Normal Triggers
Inhaled allergens
Aspirin, pulmonary infections, cold, exercise, psychological stress, inhaled irritants
Onset Childhood onset, seasonal variation
Often middle age ("late onset", usually after 30 years); tends to be more continuous and more severe; status asthmaticus is common

> The final humoral and cellular mediators of airway obstruction are common to both variants, so both are treated in a similar way.

title: 1.1.2 Pathophysiology and Pathology
content:
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY AND PATHOLOGY


PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

The pathophysiology of asthma is complex. The main component is airway inflammation:

 * Inflammation from the trachea to the terminal bronchioles, predominantly in the bronchi.
 * Cells involved: T lymphocytes, mast cells, eosinophils.
 * Associated changes: plasma exudation, oedema, smooth-muscle hypertrophy, matrix deposition, mucus plugging and epithelial damage.

Pathogenesis of asthma: Th1 / Th2 response [api/images/12V49PwfTcba/asthma-pathogenesis-th1-th2.png]

Pathogenesis of asthma: IgE-mediated cascade [api/images/TjhgJ60jIrtT/asthma-pathogenesis-ige-cascade.png]

Normal versus asthmatic airway [api/images/mVV3i9WbTN6M/asthma-normal-vs-asthmatic-airway.png]


PATHOLOGICAL PICTURE

Gross: bronchi and bronchioles contain thick secretions.

Microscopic:

 * A. Lumen of the bronchi: mucous plugs containing whorls of shed epithelium (Curschmann's spirals) and crystalloids from eosinophils (Charcot-Leyden crystals).
 * B. Wall of the bronchi:
   1. Basement membrane thickened
   2. Increased number of mucous glands
   3. Hypertrophy of the wall muscles
   4. Inflammatory infiltrate, mainly eosinophils

title: 1.1.3 Risk Factors
content:
RISK FACTORS

Risk factors that can contribute to asthma or airway hyper-reactivity:

 * Genetics: multiple gene mutations act synergistically in the pathophysiology of asthma.
 * Environmental allergens: house dust mites; animal allergens (especially cat and dog); cockroach allergens; fungi.
 * Viral respiratory tract infections.
 * Exercise, hyperventilation.
 * Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).
 * Chronic sinusitis or rhinitis.
 * Aspirin / NSAID hypersensitivity, sulfite sensitivity.
 * Work-related (occupational) asthma.
 * Obesity.
 * Environmental pollutants, tobacco smoke.
 * Occupational exposure: irritants (e.g., household sprays, paint fumes); high- and low-molecular-weight compounds (insects, plants, latex, gums, diisocyanates, anhydrides, wood dust, fluxes).
 * Emotional factors or stress.
 * Perinatal factors: prematurity, increased maternal age, maternal smoking, prenatal exposure to tobacco smoke.

title: 1.1.4 Clinical Presentation and Investigations
content:
CLINICAL PRESENTATION AND INVESTIGATIONS


CLINICAL PRESENTATION

 * Recurrent episodes of cough and wheeze after exposure to an airborne allergen or pollutant; symptoms vary in time and in intensity.
 * Troublesome cough at night or in the early morning.
 * Cough or wheeze after exercise, changes of weather, viral infections, smoke and strong odors.

Assessment of asthma symptom control [api/images/bLPZ0YICUOGC/asthma-symptom-control-assessment.png]


INVESTIGATIONS

 1. Peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR): measured on waking, before taking a bronchodilator, and before bed after a bronchodilator. Particularly useful to demonstrate the variable airflow limitation that characterizes the disease. It should not exceed 20%.
 2. Spirometry: useful especially for assessing reversibility. Asthma is diagnosed by a >15% improvement in FEV1 after inhaling a bronchodilator.
 3. Histamine or methacholine bronchial provocation test: shows airway hyper-responsiveness, found in most asthmatics. Particularly useful in patients whose main symptom is cough.
 4. Chest X-ray: no diagnostic features of asthma, although overinflation is characteristic during an acute episode.

Peak flow meter and normal PEF values [api/images/OmZT64XVDLz0/peak-flow-meter-and-normal-values.png]

title: 1.1.5 Management of Chronic Asthma
content:
MANAGEMENT OF CHRONIC ASTHMA


AIMS OF TREATMENT

 * Abolish symptoms.
 * Restore normal or best possible lung function.
 * Reduce the risk of severe attacks.
 * Minimize absence from employment.


THIS INVOLVES

 * Patient and family education and participation in treatment.
 * Avoidance of identified causes where possible (e.g., family pets, occupational agents), with rapid identification and removal of extrinsic causes.
 * Use of the lowest effective doses of convenient medications.
 * Minimizing short-term and long-term side effects.


DRUG TREATMENT: PRINCIPLES

The mainstay is drugs delivered as aerosols or powders directly into the lungs. Advantages: drugs reach the airways directly, first-pass metabolism in the liver is avoided, so lower doses are needed and systemic side effects are minimized.

Guidelines are based on three principles:

 1. Self-management with regular monitoring using PEF meters and written individual treatment plans.
 2. Asthma is an inflammatory disease, so anti-inflammatory (controller) therapy is started even in mild cases.
 3. Short-acting inhaled bronchodilators (salbutamol, terbutaline) only to relieve breakthrough symptoms. Increasing use to relieve increasing symptoms means deteriorating disease.


PREVENTERS (ANTI-INFLAMMATORY)

1. Corticosteroids

 * Actions: reduce vascular permeability and dilatation, suppress accumulation of neutrophils, reduce circulating monocytes, eosinophils and basophils, and inhibit fibroblast proliferation.
 * Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS): first-line therapy for chronic asthma and the most effective available. Reduce bronchial wall inflammation, airway hyper-responsiveness and symptoms. Side effects are usually local: oral monilial infection (candidiasis), hoarseness of voice, dysphonia.
 * Systemic corticosteroids: high doses control symptoms but cause many adverse effects outside the respiratory tract: gastritis, gastric ulcer, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, fungal infection, immunosuppression, adrenal gland suppression, Cushingoid features.

2. Leukotriene antagonists: given orally; may have a role in mild asthma or as corticosteroid-sparing drugs.

3. Immunotherapy / Anti-IgE: small, then increasing doses of pure antigen are given to a sensitive patient to interfere with the IgE-antigen reaction. Expected to work best in atopic asthma.


BRONCHODILATORS (RELIEVERS)

Drug Examples / dose Notes and side effects Inhaled short-acting β2 agonists
Salbutamol, terbutaline, fenoterol
Relax airway smooth muscle, enhance mucociliary clearance, decrease vascular permeability, may modulate mediator release from mast cells and basophils. No beneficial effect on the underlying chronic inflammation. Used as needed for symptoms.
Long-acting β2 agonists Slow-release oral salbutamol and terbutaline
Longer duration than conventional tablets. Theophylline Serum level 10-20 μg/mL
Relaxes smooth muscle by inhibiting phosphodiesterase; increases diaphragm contractility and reduces its fatigue. Below this range bronchodilatation is unlikely; above it toxicity is common.
Anticholinergics (muscarinic antagonists)
Ipratropium bromide 20-40 μg 3-4 times daily; oxitropium bromide 200 μg 2-3 times daily
Added to the regimen as regular inhaled therapy.

Side effects of β2 agonists (extremely safe, even in large doses, especially when inhaled):

 * Cardiovascular: tachycardia, increased cardiac output, inotropism, ECG changes.
 * Systemic: hypokalaemia, hyperglycaemia, increased free fatty acids, hypomagnesaemia, increased blood lactate, uterine relaxation.
 * Skeletal muscle tremor, which can be distressing.

Side effects of theophylline: nausea and vomiting; cardiac arrhythmias up to ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest; neurotoxicity (convulsions).


INHALATION DELIVERY SYSTEMS

 * Pressurized metered dose inhaler
 * Dry powder inhalers
 * Nebulizers


STEP CARE FOR CHRONIC ASTHMA IN ADULTS

Step Treatment Step 1
Inhaled short-acting β2 agonists as required. If needed more than once, go to step 2.
Step 2
Step 1 + regular low-dose inhaled steroids (beclomethasone, budesonide), the cornerstone and preferred option; or leukotriene receptor antagonist; or low-dose theophylline.
Step 3
Step 1 + high-dose inhaled steroids + long-acting inhaled β2 agonist; or high/medium-dose inhaled steroids + leukotriene receptor antagonist or theophylline.
Step 4
Step 1 + medium/high-dose inhaled steroids + long-acting β2 agonists; or medium/high-dose inhaled steroids + long-acting muscarinic antagonists + leukotriene receptor antagonist or theophylline.
Step 5
Step 4 + long-acting muscarinic antagonists, anti-IgE or anti-IL-5; or Step 4 + oral steroids.

 * Start at the step most appropriate to the initial severity.
 * A rescue course of prednisolone may be needed at any time and any step.
 * Step down only after asthma has been stable for 3-6 months.

GINA stepwise approach to asthma treatment [api/images/kO90GrDHCFlT/asthma-gina-stepwise-treatment.png]

title: 1.1.6 Acute Severe Asthma
content:
ACUTE SEVERE ASTHMA

Severe asthma that has not been controlled by the patient's usual medication.


FEATURES OF ACUTE SEVERE ASTHMA

 * Inability to complete a sentence in one breath.
 * Respiratory rate ≥ 25 breaths/min.
 * Tachycardia ≥ 110 beats/min.
 * PEFR < 50% of predicted normal or best.


LIFE-THREATENING INDICATORS

 * PEFR < 33% of predicted or best.
 * Exhaustion, confusion, coma.
 * Silent chest, cyanosis or feeble respiratory effort.
 * Bradycardia or hypotension.
 * Measure arterial blood gases if any of these are present or if oxygen saturation is < 92%.


VERY SEVERE, LIFE-THREATENING ATTACK (ABG)

 * Normal (5-6 kPa, 36-45 mmHg) or increased carbon dioxide tension.
 * Severe hypoxia: < 8 kPa (60 mmHg).
 * Low pH.


MANAGEMENT

 * Monitor pulse, BP, conscious level, O2 saturation and arterial blood gases.
 * Humidified high-flow O2 to maintain saturation > 90%.
 * β2 agonist (salbutamol) by nebulizer; can be repeated after 20 min.
 * Systemic corticosteroids, oral or IV, can be repeated according to severity (e.g., hydrocortisone 200 mg).
 * Nebulized ipratropium bromide 500 μg.
 * IV infusion of aminophylline.
 * Consider indications for intubation and mechanical ventilation; elective intubation is always better than an emergency procedure.
 * Never give sedatives unless the patient is intubated and on mechanical ventilation.
 * Chest X-ray to rule out pneumothorax.
 * If there is no improvement: add nebulized ipratropium to the nebulized β2 agonist, and give IV aminophylline or salbutamol or terbutaline.


INDICATIONS FOR MECHANICAL VENTILATION (IPPV)

 * Worsening hypoxia < 8 kPa (60 mmHg).
 * Drowsiness.
 * Unconsciousness.

title: 1.1.7 Asthma in Brief and Viva Questions
content:
ASTHMA IN BRIEF AND VIVA QUESTIONS


ASTHMA IN BRIEF

History

 * Is there reversible airway obstruction? Are the wheezing and breathlessness reversible?
 * Tightness in the chest.
 * Recurrent cough.
 * Exacerbation of cough or wheeze at night or after exercise.
 * Improvement of cough or wheeze with bronchodilators.
 * Exacerbations with fever and yellowish sputum.
 * History of atopy (eczema, hay fever).
 * History of rhinitis and nasal polyps.

Examination

 * Bilateral scattered wheeze.
 * Examine the sputum cup.
 * Comment on accessory muscles of respiration, tachycardia, pulsus paradoxus, and whether the patient can speak sentences without stopping to breathe.

Diagnosis (how to phrase it in the exam)

> This patient has a history of hay fever and bilateral scattered wheeze (lesion) due to bronchial asthma (etiology), and is breathless at rest (functional status).


QUESTIONS

Mention a few trigger factors known to aggravate asthma.
Infection; emotion; exercise; drugs (e.g., beta-blockers); external allergens.

What do you understand by the term "asthma"?
An inflammatory disorder characterized by hyper-responsiveness of the airway to various stimuli, resulting in widespread narrowing of the airway. The changes are reversible, either spontaneously or as a result of therapy.

What is intrinsic asthma? (advanced)
Non-allergic etiology, usually begins after the age of 30. Tends to be more continuous and more severe; status asthmaticus is common.

What is extrinsic asthma? (advanced)
A clearly defined history of allergy to a variety of inhaled factors; childhood onset and seasonal variation.

What are the indications for steroids in bronchial asthma? (advanced)

 * Sleep is disturbed by wheeze.
 * Morning tightness persists until midday.
 * Symptoms and peak expiratory flows progressively deteriorate each day.
 * Frequent treatment with bronchodilators.
 * Emergency, and during attacks when nebulizers are needed.

When to reduce or discontinue inhaled steroids in mild asthma? (advanced)
Early treatment with inhaled steroids gives long-lasting control of mild asthma (FEV1 more than 85% of predicted). Maintenance can usually be given at a reduced dose; discontinuation is often possible when the patient has no exacerbations.

How would you manage a patient with acute asthma? and What is the step care regimen?
See the dedicated notes: Acute Severe Asthma and Management of Chronic Asthma.

title: 1.2.1 Definition and Risk Factors
content:
DEFINITION AND RISK FACTORS

COPD has been the third most common cause of death and the fifth most common cause of disability worldwide since 2020.


DEFINITION

COPD is a common, preventable and treatable disease characterized by persistent respiratory symptoms and airflow limitation due to airway and/or alveolar abnormalities, usually caused by significant exposure to noxious particles or gases.

The chronic airflow limitation is caused by a mixture of:

 * Large airway affection by chronic bronchitis
 * Small airways disease (e.g., obstructive bronchiolitis)
 * Parenchymal destruction (emphysema)

The relative contribution of each varies from person to person.


RISK FACTORS

 * Tobacco smoke: over 90% of cases (cigarette, pipe, cigar, water-pipe, environmental tobacco smoke). The risk of death from COPD in a patient smoking 30 cigarettes daily is 20 times that of a non-smoker.
 * Indoor air pollution: biomass fuel used for cooking and heating in poorly ventilated dwellings; particularly affects women in developing countries.
 * Occupational exposures: organic and inorganic dusts, chemical agents, fumes.
 * Outdoor air pollution: adds to the total burden of inhaled particles but has a relatively small effect.
 * Genetic factors: severe hereditary deficiency of alpha-1 antitrypsin (AATD). Family members should be screened; a level < 20% of normal strongly suggests homozygous deficiency.
 * Age and gender: aging and female gender increase risk.
 * Socioeconomic status: risk is inversely related to socioeconomic status (reflects exposure to pollutants, crowding, poor nutrition, infections).
 * Chronic bronchitis: chronic inflammation of the bronchi, clinically defined as repeated attacks of cough and expectoration for more than 3 months per year for 2 successive years; may increase the frequency of total and severe exacerbations.
 * Infections: severe childhood respiratory infection is associated with reduced lung function and more respiratory symptoms in adulthood.

COPD classification by cause [api/images/mitN9vqB4mv7/copd-classification-by-cause.png]

title: 1.2.2 Pathophysiology
content:
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

 * Bronchial mucosa shows an increased number of mucus-secreting goblet cells, especially in the larger bronchi. In advanced cases the bronchi become inflamed and pus is seen in the lumen.
 * Loss of elasticity and alveolar attachments of the airways due to:
   * Emphysema: pathological dilatation and destruction of lung tissue distal to the terminal bronchiole. This reduces elastic recoil, so the airways collapse during expiration.
   * Inflammation and scarring narrow the small airways.
   * Mucus secretion blocks the airways.
 * Processes important in pathogenesis: inflammation, protease/antiprotease imbalance, oxidative stress, apoptosis.
 * Pathologic changes occur in central airways, peripheral airways, lung parenchyma and pulmonary vasculature: destruction of alveolar tissue, inflammation, oedema, airway mucus and fibrosis.
 * Physiologic changes: decreased maximal expiratory airflow, lung hyperinflation, abnormal alveolar gas exchange, pulmonary vascular disease.
 * Systemic component: increased incidence of osteoporosis, skeletal muscle dysfunction and coronary artery disease, indicating systemic inflammation.

Summary: each mechanism narrows the small airways and causes air trapping, leading to hyperinflation of the lungs and breathlessness.

title: 1.2.3 Chronic Bronchitis (Pathology)
content:
CHRONIC BRONCHITIS (PATHOLOGY)


ETIOPATHOGENESIS

The two most important causes are cigarette smoking and atmospheric pollution. Other contributing factors: occupation, infection, familial and genetic factors.

Prolonged cigarette smoking acts on the lungs by:

 1. Impairing ciliary movement.
 2. Inhibiting the function of alveolar macrophages.
 3. Causing hypertrophy and hyperplasia of mucus-secreting glands.
 4. Causing considerable obstruction of small airways.
 5. Stimulating the vagus, causing bronchoconstriction.


MORPHOLOGY

Gross: the bronchial wall is thickened, hyperemic and oedematous. The lumina of bronchi and bronchioles may contain mucus plugs and purulent exudate.

Microscopic: chronic bronchitis is defined clinically but also histologically by an increased Reid index.

 * Reid index = ratio of the thickness of the submucosal mucus glands (hypertrophy and hyperplasia) in the cartilage-containing large airways to the thickness of the total bronchial wall.
 * The bronchial epithelium may show squamous metaplasia and dysplasia.
 * There is little chronic inflammatory cell infiltrate.

Increased Reid index in chronic bronchitis [api/images/ThDs1dKjvAuV/chronic-bronchitis-reid-index.png]

title: 1.2.4 Emphysema (Pathology)
content:
EMPHYSEMA (PATHOLOGY)


DEFINITION (WHO)

Permanent dilatation of the air spaces distal to the terminal bronchioles together with destruction of the walls of the dilated air spaces.

Emphysema is defined morphologically, while chronic bronchitis is defined clinically.


CLASSIFICATION

Type Part of the acinus affected Notes 1. Centriacinar (centrilobular)
Central / proximal part
Usually coexists with chronic bronchitis; mostly in smokers and coal miners' pneumoconiosis
2. Panacinar (panlobular) All portions of the acinus (not of the entire lung)
Most often with α1-antitrypsin deficiency in middle-aged smokers
3. Paraseptal (distal acinar) Distal part; proximal part normal
Along the pleura and perilobular septa; seldom associated with COPD; common cause of spontaneous pneumothorax in young adults
4. Irregular (para-cicatricial) Around scars
Most common form; seen surrounding scars from any cause 5. Mixed (unclassified)
More than one type Quite often in the same lung

Normal acinus compared with centriacinar and panacinar emphysema [api/images/LLoAKvaVbOx9/emphysema-types-acinus.png]


ETIOPATHOGENESIS

 * The commonest form of COPD is the combination of chronic bronchitis and emphysema. Chronic bronchitis does not always lead to emphysema, and not all emphysema has features of chronic bronchitis.
 * The two are linked mainly through common causes: tobacco smoke and air pollutants. Less important: occupational exposure, infection, familial and genetic factors.
 * The key event, destruction of alveolar walls, is not linked to bronchial changes but to deficiency of serum α1-antitrypsin: the protease-antiprotease hypothesis.


PROTEASE-ANTIPROTEASE HYPOTHESIS

 * α1-antitrypsin (α1-AT, α1-protease inhibitor) is synthesized in the liver and distributed in blood, tissue fluids and macrophages.
 * Its normal function is to inhibit proteases, mainly elastases derived from neutrophils.
 * Neutrophil elastase can digest lung parenchyma, but is normally held in check by the anti-elastase effect of α1-AT.
 * When α1-AT is deficient (or overwhelmed, e.g., by smoke), elastase destroys the alveolar walls.

title: 1.2.5 Clinical Features
content:
CLINICAL FEATURES


HISTORY

 * Lifelong smoking history; quantify exposure to environmental and occupational risk factors.
 * Most common symptoms: dyspnea, cough, sputum production, wheezing. Dyspnea on exertion progresses gradually over time.
 * Significant nocturnal symptoms should lead to a search for comorbidities: GERD, congestive heart failure, sleep-disordered breathing.

Characteristic symptoms:

 * Productive cough with white or clear sputum.
 * Wheeze and breathlessness, progressing until even mild exertion such as getting dressed causes it.
 * Frequent infective exacerbations, giving purulent sputum.
 * Systemic effects: hypertension, osteoporosis, depression, metabolic problems leading to weight loss and muscle wasting with weakness.


SIGNS

 * Mild disease: may be no signs, or only quiet wheezes throughout the chest.
 * Severe disease:
   * Tachypnea with prolonged expiration.
   * Use of accessory muscles of respiration; intercostal indrawing on inspiration.
   * Pursing of the lips on expiration.
   * Poor chest expansion; hyperinflated lungs; loss of normal cardiac and liver dullness.

title: 1.2.6 Diagnosis and Assessment
content:
DIAGNOSIS AND ASSESSMENT


KEY POINTS

 * Consider COPD in any patient with progressive dyspnea, chronic cough or sputum production, with a history of exposure to risk factors.
 * Spirometry is required to make the diagnosis: a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC < 0.70 confirms persistent airflow limitation.
 * Goals of assessment: determine the severity of airflow limitation, the impact on health status, and the risk of future events (exacerbations, hospital admissions, death), in order to guide therapy.
 * Look for systemic manifestations: cardiovascular disease, skeletal muscle dysfunction, metabolic syndrome, osteoporosis, depression, anxiety, lung cancer.

Clinical indicators for considering a diagnosis of COPD [api/images/EeKucry9dTIg/copd-clinical-indicators.png]


INVESTIGATIONS

 * Lung function tests: airflow limitation; FEV1:FVC ratio < 70%; airflow limitation is irreversible to some extent (change in FEV1 usually < 15%, or < 200 mL).
 * Chest X-ray: often normal. In advanced cases: overinflation with low flattened diaphragms, sometimes large bullae.
 * High-resolution CT: particularly to show emphysematous bullae.
 * Blood gases: often normal at rest. In advanced cases hypoxemia, possibly hypercapnia.
 * ECG: in advanced cor pulmonale the P wave is taller (P pulmonale).
 * Echocardiogram: to assess cardiac function when dyspnea is disproportionate.
 * α1-antitrypsin levels and genotype: especially in premature disease or non-smokers.


STAGES OF COPD (GOLD)

Stage Severity Function Symptoms of breathlessness I Mild
FEV1/FVC < 70% and FEV1 ≥ 80% predicted None or mild II Moderate
FEV1/FVC < 70% and 50% ≤ FEV1 < 80% predicted On exertion III Severe
FEV1/FVC < 70% and 30% ≤ FEV1 < 50% predicted
On minimal exertion, e.g., dressing IV Very severe
FEV1/FVC < 70% and FEV1 < 30% predicted, or FEV1 < 50% plus respiratory failure
At rest

title: 1.2.7 Management of COPD
content:
MANAGEMENT OF COPD


I. PHARMACOLOGIC THERAPY

Used to reduce symptoms, reduce the frequency and severity of exacerbations, and improve exercise tolerance and health status.

1. Bronchodilators (increase FEV1 and/or change other spirometry variables)

Class Mechanism Examples Adverse effects β2-agonists
Relax airway smooth muscle by stimulating β2-adrenergic receptors, increasing cyclic AMP
SABA: salbutamol. LABA: formoterol and salmeterol (twice daily); indacaterol, olodaterol, vilanterol (once daily)
Resting sinus tachycardia, may precipitate arrhythmias; exaggerated somatic tremor
Antimuscarinics Block bronchoconstrictor effect of acetylcholine on M3 receptors
SAMA: ipratropium, oxitropium. LAMA: tiotropium, aclidinium, glycopyrronium bromide, umeclidinium
Poorly absorbed so few systemic effects; main one is dry mouth Methylxanthines
Theophylline (metabolized by cytochrome P450; clearance declines with age)
Toxicity is dose-related; small therapeutic ratio, most benefit only near toxic doses

2. Anti-inflammatory agents

 * Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) combined with a long-acting bronchodilator: in moderate to very severe COPD with exacerbations, ICS + LABA is more effective than either alone for lung function, health status and reducing exacerbations.
 * Adverse effects of ICS: oral candidiasis, hoarse voice, skin bruising, pneumonia.

3. Antibiotics: patients can be given a supply to start as soon as the sputum turns yellow or green.

4. Mucolytics and antioxidants (NAC, carbocysteine): reduce sputum viscosity and can reduce acute exacerbations.


II. NON-PHARMACOLOGIC THERAPY

 * Smoking cessation: essential. Even late in the disease it slows deterioration and delays disability and death.
 * Pulmonary rehabilitation: modest increase in exercise capacity, less breathlessness, better well-being.
 * Vaccines: yearly influenza vaccine and one dose of pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine.
 * α1-antitrypsin replacement: weekly or monthly infusions for patients with serum levels below 310 mg/L and abnormal lung function.
 * Surgery: large emphysematous bullae can be treated by bullectomy, allowing collapsed adjacent lung to re-expand.
 * Lung transplantation.

Stepwise management of COPD [api/images/y5agPaTpnBgX/copd-stepwise-management.png]

title: 1.2.8 Complications
content:
COMPLICATIONS OF COPD

 1. Respiratory failure: occurs in the later stages.
 2. Cor pulmonale: heart disease secondary to lung disease. Characterized by pulmonary hypertension, right ventricular hypertrophy and eventually right heart failure.
    * On examination: ankle oedema, right hypochondrial tenderness, prominent parasternal heave (right ventricular hypertrophy), loud pulmonary second sound.
    * Treatment: diuretics and ACE inhibitors.
 3. Pneumothorax.
 4. Bronchiectasis (see Bronchiectasis).

title: 1.3.1 Definition and Etiology
content:
DEFINITION AND ETIOLOGY


DEFINITION

The term bronchiectasis describes abnormal and permanently dilated airways. The bronchial walls become inflamed, thickened and irreversibly damaged. The muco-ciliary transport mechanism is impaired and frequent bacterial infections follow.

Clinically: cough with production of large amounts of sputum, and dilated, thickened bronchi seen on CT. It is one of the suppurative lung diseases.


ETIOLOGY

 * Congenital: deficiency of bronchial wall elements; increased mucus viscosity, as in cystic fibrosis.
 * Mechanical bronchial obstruction
   * Intraluminal: foreign body, inspissated mucus, post-tuberculous stenosis, tumor
   * Extraluminal: lymph node, tumor
 * Bacterial and viral pneumonia: including pertussis, measles, Klebsiella, staphylococcus, Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
 * Diffuse diseases of the lung parenchyma: e.g., idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, sarcoidosis.
 * Immune deficiency
   * Primary: pan-hypogammaglobulinaemia, selective immunoglobulin deficiencies (IgA and IgG2)
   * Secondary: HIV and malignancy
 * Muco-ciliary clearance defects (genetic): primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener's syndrome: dextrocardia and situs inversus), cystic fibrosis.

title: 1.3.2 Pathology
content:
PATHOLOGY


PATHOLOGICAL FEATURES

 * Permanent dilation of the bronchi and bronchioles caused by destruction of the muscle and elastic supporting tissue, resulting from or associated with chronic necrotizing infection.
 * Once developed, it gives a symptom complex dominated by cough and expectoration of conspicuous amounts of purulent sputum.


PREDISPOSING CONDITIONS AND PATHOGENESIS

 * Bronchial obstruction by tumors, foreign bodies, mucus impaction: bronchiectasis is localized to the segment with the occluded bronchus. Atopic asthma and chronic bronchitis may be complicated by bronchiectasis.
 * Two processes are critical: chronic persistent infection and obstruction.
 * With obstruction, normal clearance is hampered, so secondary infection follows, which weakens the bronchial wall and leads to dilatation. Bronchogenic cancer and foreign bodies impair clearance of secretions and give fertile soil for superimposed infection. The resulting inflammation damages the wall and causes irreversible dilation.
 * Persistent necrotizing inflammation in small and large airways may cause obstructive secretions, peribronchial fibrosis and traction scarring.


MORPHOLOGY

Gross

 * Bilateral, more common in the lower lobes, with patchy distribution.
 * Dilatation may be cylindrical, fusiform, tortuous or saccular.
 * Enlarged dilated bronchi near the pleura.
 * Lumen contains pus; mucosa shows ulceration; surrounding alveoli are fibrotic.
 * Pleura shows pleurisy then fibrosis.
 * Enlarged draining lymph nodes.

Microscopic

 1. Bronchial epithelium may be normal, ulcerated, or show squamous metaplasia.
 2. Bronchial wall shows infiltration by acute and chronic inflammatory cells and destruction of musculoelastic tissue.

Types of bronchiectasis: cylindrical, varicose, fusiform, saccular [api/images/BggZJ8EjKg51/bronchiectasis-types-varicose-cylindrical-saccular.png]

title: 1.3.3 Clinical Features and Investigations
content:
CLINICAL FEATURES AND INVESTIGATIONS


CLINICAL FEATURES

 * Early: yellow or green sputum only after an infection.
 * As it worsens: continuous production of increasing amounts of sputum, foul-smelling, thick, khaki-colored, and varying with position.
 * Persistent halitosis, recurrent febrile episodes with malaise, episodes of pneumonia.
 * Breathlessness from airflow limitation.
 * Hemoptysis: bloodstained sputum or massive hemorrhage.
 * Clubbing; coarse crackles over the infected areas, usually the lung bases.


INVESTIGATIONS

 * Chest X-ray: may be normal, or show dilated bronchi with thickened walls and sometimes multiple fluid-containing cysts.
 * High-resolution CT: bronchial dilatation with loss of airway tapering at the periphery, wall thickening, cysts at the ends of bronchioles; sensitivity 97%.
 * Sputum culture and sensitivity: essential for treatment. Major pathogens: Staph. aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, H. influenzae, anaerobes. Others: Strep. pneumoniae, Klebsiella pneumoniae.
 * Sweat electrolytes: if cystic fibrosis is suspected.

title: 1.3.4 Treatment and Complications
content:
TREATMENT AND COMPLICATIONS


TREATMENT

 * Postural drainage: essential; the patient is trained by physiotherapists to tip into a position with the affected lobe(s) uppermost at least 3 times daily for 10-20 minutes.
 * Antibiotics: if sputum remains yellow or green despite regular physiotherapy, or if lung function deteriorates despite bronchodilators.
 * Bronchodilators: in patients with demonstrable airflow limitation.
 * Anti-inflammatory agents: inhaled or oral steroids can slow progression.
 * Mucolytics and antioxidants (NAC, carbocysteine): reduce sputum viscosity and acute exacerbations.
 * Surgery: rarely practical because the disease is seldom sufficiently localized. Lung or heart-lung transplantation is sometimes required.


COMPLICATIONS

 * Severe, massive, life-threatening hemoptysis: originates from the high-pressure systemic bronchial arteries; mortality 25%.
 * Pneumonia
 * Pneumothorax
 * Empyema
 * Metastatic cerebral abscess

title: 1.3.5 Bronchiectasis in Brief and Viva Questions
content:
BRONCHIECTASIS IN BRIEF AND VIVA QUESTIONS


IN BRIEF

History

 * Cough with copious purulent sputum, recurrent hemoptysis.
 * Intermittent fever and night sweats.
 * History of recurrent chest infections.
 * Weight loss.

Examination

 * Copious purulent expectoration (check the sputum cup).
 * Finger clubbing.
 * Bilateral coarse, late inspiratory crackles.

Diagnosis (exam phrasing)

> This patient has bilateral, coarse, late inspiratory crackles with purulent sputum (lesion) due to bronchiectasis (etiology).


QUESTIONS

What is bronchiectasis?
A chronic necrotizing infection of the bronchi and bronchioles leading to abnormal, permanent dilatation of the airways.

Causes?

 * Post pneumonia, measles, pertussis, tuberculosis.
 * Mechanical bronchial obstruction (TB lymph nodes, carcinoma, nodal compression).
 * Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis.
 * Gamma-globulin deficiency (congenital or acquired).
 * Immotile cilia syndrome (Kartagener's).
 * Cystic fibrosis.
 * Neuropathic disorders (Riley-Day syndrome, Chagas' disease).
 * Idiopathic.

Investigations?
HRCT chest, fiberoptic bronchoscopy for endobronchial lesions, sputum culture, CXR for follow-up.

Treatment?
Postural drainage, antibiotics, bronchodilators, surgery in selected cases.

Complications? (advanced)
Pneumonia, pleurisy, pleural effusion, pneumothorax; sinusitis; hemoptysis; brain abscess; amyloidosis.

Major respiratory pathogens?
Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

How can CT assess bronchiectasis? (advanced)
HRCT at end-expiration suggests small airway disease may be an early feature. Conventional CT has 60-80% sensitivity; HRCT more than 90%.

Standard versus high-resolution CT? (advanced)
Standard CT slices are 10 mm thick; HRCT slices are 1-2 mm thick with high spatial resolution reconstruction.

Associated abnormalities? (advanced)

 * Congenital absence of bronchial cartilage (Williams-Campbell syndrome).
 * Tracheobronchomegaly (Mounier-Kuhn syndrome).
 * Obstructive azoospermia with chronic sinopulmonary infection (Young's syndrome).
 * Situs inversus and paranasal sinusitis (Kartagener's syndrome).

Indication for surgery? (advanced)
Bronchiectasis localized to a single lobe or segment, with no clinical, bronchographic or CT evidence of disease elsewhere in the lung.

Common sites of localized disease? (advanced) Left lower lobe and lingula.

Reid's classification (advanced)
Described in 1950 from correlation of pathology with bronchography. All three types can coexist in one patient.

 * Cylindrical: uniformly dilated bronchi that do not taper but end abruptly (plugging of smaller bronchi by thick mucus). Dilated > 2 mm.
 * Varicose: dilated bronchi with irregular bulging contours like a varicose vein; bulbous terminations; reduced subdivisions.
 * Cystic (saccular): the most severe; sharply reduced subdivisions and dilated bronchi ending in cystic pus-filled cavities.

title: 1.4.1 Definition, Pathophysiology and Presentation
content:
DEFINITION, PATHOPHYSIOLOGY AND PRESENTATION


DEFINITION

 * A localized area of lung suppuration leading to necrosis of the pulmonary parenchyma, with or without cavity formation.
 * May be single or multiple, acute or chronic (> 1 month), primary or secondary.
 * May occur spontaneously, but more commonly an underlying disease exists.


PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

 * Most are the result of aspiration pneumonia.
 * Predisposing factors:
   * Dental disease
   * Impaired consciousness: alcohol, post-anesthesia, dysphagia
   * Diabetes
   * Bronchial carcinoma (with bronchial obstruction)
   * Secondary to pneumonia (cavitation in about 16% of Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia)
   * Immunocompromise
   * Septic embolization (right-sided endocarditis due to Staph. aureus in intravenous drug abusers)
 * The bacterial inoculum reaches the lung parenchyma, often in a dependent area.
 * Cavitation occurs when necrosis communicates with a bronchus: air enters, necrotic material is coughed up, forming an air-fluid level.
 * Bronchial obstruction leads to atelectasis, stasis and infection, which can predispose to abscess formation.


PRESENTATION

 * Often insidious onset
 * Productive cough, hemoptysis
 * Breathlessness
 * Fevers, night sweats
 * Non-specific features of chronic infection: anemia, weight loss, malaise (especially in the elderly)
 * Foul sputum or purulent pleural fluid

title: 1.4.2 Diagnosis and Investigations
content:
DIAGNOSIS AND INVESTIGATIONS

The diagnosis is usually made from the history together with a cavity with an air-fluid level on chest X-ray.


INVESTIGATIONS

 * Microbiological culture, ideally before starting antibiotics. Also useful to exclude tuberculosis. Blood cultures; sputum or bronchoscopy specimen (BAL needed).
 * Imaging:
   * CXR may show consolidation, cavitation, air-fluid level.
   * CT if the diagnosis is in doubt; it also defines the exact position of the abscess (useful for physiotherapy, or if surgery is considered, which is rarely needed).


DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS OF A CAVITATING MASS (WITH OR WITHOUT AIR-FLUID LEVEL)

 * Cavitating carcinoma, primary or metastatic
 * Cavitary tuberculosis
 * Sarcoidosis

title: 1.4.3 Management and Complications
content:
MANAGEMENT AND COMPLICATIONS


MANAGEMENT

 * Antibiotics: infections are usually mixed, so cover aerobes and anaerobes, including β-lactamase inhibitors (e.g., co-amoxiclav and clindamycin) and metronidazole for anaerobes. Long courses are needed: typically 1-2 weeks IV followed by 2-6 weeks oral.
 * Physiotherapy for drainage is common, given the purulent sputum.
 * Surgery is rarely required if antibiotic treatment is appropriate. Reserved for complicated infections failing standard treatment after at least 6 weeks. Lobectomy or pneumonectomy is occasionally needed when severe infection leaves a large volume of damaged lung that is hard to sterilize.


COMPLICATIONS

 * Hemorrhage, which can be massive and life-threatening, is an indication for urgent surgery.

title: Definition and Classification
content:
DEFINITION AND CLASSIFICATION


DEFINITION

 * ILD is also known as diffuse parenchymal lung disease, affecting the interstitium: the tissue and space around the air sacs of the lungs. It involves the alveolar epithelium, pulmonary capillary endothelium, basement membrane, and perivascular and perilymphatic tissues.
 * The interstitium is a lace-like network of tissue throughout the lungs that supports the alveoli. Tiny blood vessels run through it, allowing gas exchange between blood and air. Normally it is so thin it cannot be seen on a chest X-ray.
 * The interstitial compartment is the area between the alveolar epithelial and capillary endothelial basement membranes.
 * The term ILD is used to distinguish these diseases from obstructive airway diseases.
 * Fibrotic ILDs often have nonspecific, overlapping clinical and radiological features, so diagnosis is challenging. A confident diagnosis may need a surgical lung biopsy, which carries substantial risk and may still be nonspecific. About 10-20% of fibrotic ILD patients have no clear diagnosis and are labeled unclassifiable ILD.

The pulmonary interstitium [api/images/rcO6XyFatHZH/ild-pulmonary-interstitium.png]


CLASSIFICATION BY CAUSE

Cause Examples 1. Occupational
Inorganic: coal workers' pneumoconiosis, silicosis, asbestosis, berylliosis, byssinosis. Organic: hypersensitivity pneumonitis
Non-occupational Sarcoidosis; idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis 2. Drug-induced
Antibiotics, chemotherapeutic drugs, antiarrhythmic agents, statins
3. Connective tissue disease
Systemic sclerosis, polymyositis, dermatomyositis, SLE, rheumatoid arthritis
4. Infection Atypical pneumonia, tuberculosis, viral pneumonia

title: Clinical Features and Investigations
content:
CLINICAL FEATURES AND INVESTIGATIONS


HOW TO SUSPECT ILD

 1. A detailed history looking for occupational exposures and signs of the conditions listed in the classification is the most important part of the workup.
 2. Onset at age 50 or older (IPF), dry cough, dyspnea, end-inspiratory rales.
 3. Pulmonary function tests usually show a restrictive defect with decreased diffusion capacity (DLCO).


MAIN CLINICAL FEATURES

 * Progressive breathlessness, non-productive cough and cyanosis, which eventually lead to respiratory failure, pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale.
 * Gross finger clubbing in two-thirds of cases.
 * Fine bilateral end-inspiratory crackles on auscultation.


INVESTIGATIONS

 * Chest X-ray: usually the first test, but can be normal early. Initially a diffuse ground-glass pattern, then reticulonodular shadowing.
 * High-resolution CT (HRCT): the preferred modality. Conventional CT examines 7-10 mm slices at 10 mm intervals; HRCT examines 1-1.5 mm slices at 10 mm intervals, giving about 10 times more resolution. ILDs can be classified by radiologic pattern. Associated findings: pleural effusion or thickening, pulmonary edema, lymphadenopathy.
 * Respiratory function tests: restrictive ventilatory defect: lung volumes are reduced; FEV1/FVC ratio is normal to high (both values reduced).
 * Carbon monoxide gas transfer (DLCO): reduced.
 * Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): in healthy adults BAL fluid has mostly alveolar macrophages with few lymphocytes, neutrophils and eosinophils. In ILD the cell counts change, but usually nonspecifically.
 * Lung biopsy: needed if history and imaging are not clearly suggestive, or if malignancy cannot be excluded. Trans-bronchial biopsy is usually unhelpful; surgical lung biopsy is often required.

title: Treatment and Complications
content:
TREATMENT AND COMPLICATIONS


TREATMENT

ILD is not one disease but many pathological processes, so treatment differs for each disease.

 * Avoid the occupational exposure if a specific cause is found.
 * Stop the causative drug if a drug cause is suspected.
 * Many cases of unknown or connective-tissue cause are treated with steroids; some respond to immunosuppressants.
 * Patients with hypoxemia may be given supplemental oxygen; oxygen therapy for complicating respiratory failure.
 * Pulmonary rehabilitation appears useful.
 * Lung transplantation is an option if ILD progresses despite therapy, in appropriately selected patients.


COMPLICATIONS

 1. Pulmonary hypertension
 2. Acute exacerbation of pulmonary fibrosis
 3. Respiratory infection
 4. Acute coronary syndrome
 5. Thromboembolic disease
 6. Adverse medication effects
 7. Lung cancer

title: Definition, Epidemiology and Immunopathology
content:
DEFINITION, EPIDEMIOLOGY AND IMMUNOPATHOLOGY


DEFINITION

A multisystem granulomatous disorder, commonly affecting young adults, usually presenting with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, pulmonary infiltration, and skin or eye lesions.

First described more than 140 years ago, its cause remains unknown. By extension from other granulomatous diseases, it is thought to start with an antigen processed by an antigen-presenting cell.


EPIDEMIOLOGY AND ETIOLOGY

 * More common in women than men, at almost 2:1.
 * In the United States: more common in African Americans than whites, less common in Hispanics and Asians.
 * Seems more common in the eastern third of the United States, which may just reflect where African Americans live.


IMMUNOPATHOLOGY

 1. The antigen-presenting cell (APC) presents the antigen through an HLA class II molecule to a restricted set of T-cell receptors on a T lymphocyte, usually CD4+.
 2. This polarizes the T cells to a T helper phenotype.
 3. Followed by monocyte recruitment, T-cell proliferation and differentiation.
 4. Leading to the sarcoid granuloma: focal accumulations of epithelioid cells, macrophages and lymphocytes (mainly T cells).

title: Pathology
content:
PATHOLOGY

Morphology

 * The histopathologic hallmark is non-caseating granulomatous inflammation, irrespective of the organ involved.
 * A compact collection of epithelioid histiocytes, rimmed by an outer zone composed largely of CD4+ T cells. Occasionally multinucleated giant cells.
 * At the periphery there is a thin layer of laminated fibroblasts. Their progressive expansion replaces the whole granuloma with a hyalinized scar.

Two other features:

 * Schaumann bodies: laminated concretions of calcium and proteins.
 * Asteroid bodies: satellite inclusions enclosed within the giant cells.

Lungs are involved in 90% of cases; lesions occur in the interstitium and around bronchioles and venules. In 5% the lesions are replaced by interstitial fibrosis, giving honeycomb lung with pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale.

Sarcoid granuloma: non-caseating granulomas, asteroid body, giant cell [api/images/jlg6TDyuajht/sarcoidosis-granuloma-histology.png]

In lymph node: non-caseating epithelioid cell granulomas with a paucity of lymphocytes; a giant cell with inclusions can be seen.

title: Clinical Features
content:
CLINICAL FEATURES


GENERAL

 * May present with no symptoms, more commonly in white than Black patients. Consider sarcoidosis also in asymptomatic patients with hilar or mediastinal adenopathy and/or diffuse parenchymal opacities on imaging.
 * Ask about family history: prevalence is much higher in first-degree relatives.
 * Peak incidence in the third and fourth decades, with female preponderance.
 * Can affect many organs; the most common presentation is respiratory, as in ILD.
 * Fever, fatigue, weight loss; peripheral lymphadenopathy with hepatic enlargement and splenomegaly.
 * Neurological involvement is rare but well recognized and can mimic many conditions.
 * Bone and joint: arthralgia.
 * Eyes: anterior uveitis is common.
 * Skin: the most common manifestation is erythema nodosum.
 * Cardiac: rare, causing ventricular dysrhythmias, conduction defects and cardiomyopathy; it is the most common cause of mortality.


PRESENTATIONS THAT CAN BE ASSUMED TO BE SARCOIDOSIS WITHOUT TISSUE CONFIRMATION

(As long as other data do not suggest an alternative diagnosis.)

 1. Lupus pernio
 2. Löfgren syndrome: bilateral hilar adenopathy on chest radiograph + erythema nodosum + periarticular inflammation or arthritis of the ankles.
 3. Heerfordt syndrome: uveitis + parotitis + fever (often).
 4. Bilateral hilar adenopathy on chest radiograph without symptoms.
 5. Positive panda sign (parotid and lacrimal gland uptake) and lambda sign (bilateral hilar and right paratracheal lymph node uptake) on gallium-67 scan.


CHEST DISEASE

 * More than 90% have thoracic involvement with an abnormal CXR.
 * Can be an incidental CXR finding in ~30%. Spontaneous remission in two-thirds; 10-30% have a chronic course.
 * At least two distinct courses:
   * Löfgren's syndrome: mild acute, usually non-progressive disease. Fever, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, erythema nodosum, arthralgia. Particularly in Caucasians. Good prognosis; resolves completely and spontaneously in 80% within 1-2 years. A minority develop lung disease.
   * Persistent progressive infiltrative lung disease.
 * Hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy: may be asymptomatic or cause cough or chest pain; often bilateral and symmetrical; may have malaise and arthralgia; benign course. Exclude TB and lymphoma (may need HRCT and lymph node aspirate or biopsy).
 * Interstitial lung involvement: may be asymptomatic or cause dyspnea, cough, chest ache or pain, malaise, fatigue. Rarely crackles or clubbing. Infiltrates on CXR can return to normal or progress to fibrosis and respiratory failure. Lung function may be normal or show a restrictive defect with reduced transfer factor.
 * Differential diagnosis: other ILD, malignancy, infection.

content:
STAGING AND INVESTIGATIONS


RADIOLOGICAL CLASSIFICATION OF THORACIC SARCOIDOSIS

Sarcoidosis chest X-ray and CT, stage 3 [api/images/4BuHa4JW7Nwf/sarcoidosis-cxr-ct-stage-3.png]


INVESTIGATIONS

 * Imaging: chest X-ray and HRCT assess diffuse parenchymal involvement and detect small nodules.
 * Full blood count: mild normochromic normocytic anemia with raised ESR or CRP.
 * Serum biochemistry: serum calcium often raised.
 * Bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy: the most useful investigation; shows non-caseating granulomas.
 * Serum ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) elevated: useful to assess disease activity.
 * Lung function: restrictive defect in pulmonary infiltration: decreased TLC, decreased FEV1 and FVC, decreased gas transfer. Usually normal in extrapulmonary disease or hilar adenopathy only.

title: Treatment
content:
TREATMENT

 * Many patients are asymptomatic and many have spontaneous resolution within 6 months of diagnosis, so not all need initial therapy.
 * The decision to treat is usually based on symptoms and, when the lungs are involved, a decline in pulmonary function.


CORTICOSTEROIDS

 * Remain the most widely used, best documented and most effective treatment.
 * Many patients need treatment for a prolonged time (> 1 year), so steroid-sparing medications should be considered early.
 * Prednisolone 30 mg for 6 weeks, then reduced to alternate-day prednisolone 15 mg for 6-12 months, according to response.

title: 2.2 Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis
content:
HYPERSENSITIVITY PNEUMONITIS (HP)


DEFINITION

A group of lung diseases caused by inhalation of an organic antigen to which the individual has been previously sensitized. Previously termed extrinsic allergic alveolitis.

Divided by time course:

 * Acute HP: follows a short exposure to a high antigen concentration; usually reversible.
 * Chronic HP: follows chronic exposure to a low antigen dose; less reversible.
 * The two may overlap, and subacute forms are recognized.

Causes of hypersensitivity pneumonitis [api/images/CrdWEm8ro9Li/hp-causes-table.png]


PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

 * Not fully understood. May involve T-cell mediated immunity and granuloma formation (type IV hypersensitivity) and/or antibody-antigen immune complex formation (type III hypersensitivity).
 * It is not an atopic disease: no rise in tissue eosinophils or IgE (type I hypersensitivity). This may partly be due to the small particle size of the antigens, which deposit more distally in the air spaces than the larger particles associated with asthma.
 * Histology: interstitial inflammatory infiltrate, often with bronchiolitis and organizing pneumonia. Non-caseating granulomata are often present and typically ill-defined and single (in sarcoidosis the granulomata are well-defined and grouped subpleurally or near bronchi).
 * Chronic HP shows fibrosis, and often no granulomata or airway involvement, particularly if exposure has ceased.


DIAGNOSIS

 * Based on history of antigen exposure plus typical clinical and HRCT features.
 * Most useful clinical features: onset of symptoms 4-8 hours after exposure and a history of recurrent episodes of symptoms.


TREATMENT

 * Prednisolone 40-60 mg daily for up to a month, then slowly reduce the dose over several months.
 * (Avoiding further exposure to the antigen is covered in the ILD treatment note.)

title: 2.3 Pneumoconioses (Occupational Lung Diseases)
content:
PNEUMOCONIOSES (OCCUPATIONAL LUNG DISEASES)

Pneumoconiosis = lung diseases caused by inhalation of dust, mostly at work (pneumo = lung; conis = dust in Greek). Also called dust diseases or occupational lung diseases.


FACTORS DETERMINING THE EXTENT OF DAMAGE

 1. Size and shape of the particles.
 2. Their solubility and physicochemical composition.
 3. The amount of dust retained in the lungs.
 4. Host factors: efficiency of clearance mechanisms and immune status.

Anthracosis is not a true lung disease: it is the common, benign, asymptomatic accumulation of carbon dust in the lungs due to atmospheric pollution and cigarette smoke.


PATHOGENESIS OF THE THREE COMMON FORMS

Form Pathogenesis A. Coal workers' pneumoconiosis
The commonest form; from inhaling coal dust, especially in coal miners. Macrophages phagocytose large amounts of dust, which pass into the interstitial tissue and aggregate around the respiratory bronchiole, causing focal dust emphysema.
B. Silicosis
Tiny silica particles are toxic to macrophages. Dead macrophages release fibrogenic factor, eventually forming the silicotic nodule.
C. Asbestosis
Asbestos fibers initiate extensive interstitial fibrosis and form asbestos bodies.

Pathogenesis of coal workers pneumoconiosis, silicosis and asbestosis [api/images/fQZ6WSPVltSE/pneumoconiosis-pathogenesis.png]

The clinical features, investigations and treatment of these diseases follow the general approach in ILD Clinical Features and Investigations and ILD Treatment.

title: Definition, Classification and Routes of Infection
content:
DEFINITION, CLASSIFICATION AND ROUTES OF INFECTION


DEFINITION

A syndrome of inflammation of the lung parenchyma caused by acute infection by a wide variety of microorganisms, characterized by clinical and/or radiological signs of consolidation of part or parts of one or both lungs.

 * The lung and tracheobronchial tree are usually sterile below the larynx, so an infecting agent must reach this site through a breach in host defenses.
 * Pneumonia is predisposed by any condition that:
   1. reduces or suppresses the cough,
   2. impairs mucociliary activity,
   3. reduces effective phagocytic activity of alveolar macrophages and neutrophils,
   4. impairs immunoglobulin production.

Pneumonia is a lower respiratory tract infection caused by inability to clear pathogens from the lower airway and alveoli. Cytokines and local inflammatory markers are released, causing further damage through an inflammatory cascade, accumulation of white blood cells and fluid congestion, leading to pus in the parenchyma.

The IDSA defines pneumonia as a new lung infiltrate with other clinical evidence supporting infection: new fever, purulent sputum, leukocytosis, and decline in oxygenation.

Lower respiratory infections remain the most common cause of death from communicable disease. Pneumonia is the fourth leading cause of death worldwide, claiming 2.6 million lives in 2019.


CLASSIFICATION

Basis Types Anatomical Lobar, segmental, bronchopneumonia Etiology
Bacterial, atypical bacterial, viral Epidemiological
Community-acquired, hospital-acquired, ventilator-associated


HOW PATHOGENS REACH THE LUNG

 * Microaspiration of secretions containing oropharyngeal flora (occurs in healthy people during sleep). Increased when cough is depressed: after surgery, general anesthesia, tracheostomy, endotracheal or nasogastric tube.
 * Inhalation from the environment, a nebulizer or anesthetic circuit: small-particle aerosols are important in transmission of viral infections and Legionella.
 * Blood spread: Gram-negative and staphylococcal bacteremia. Susceptible: patients with IV cannulae, temporary pacing wires, chronic hemodialysis.
 * Colonization of an already diseased lower respiratory tract (chronic bronchitis, emphysema, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis), which may cause acute exacerbations.
 * Direct spread from an adjacent extrapulmonary site: mediastinum, spine, chest wall, abdominal cavity.

title: Pathology of Pneumonia
content:
PATHOLOGY OF PNEUMONIA


LOBAR PNEUMONIA: FOUR STAGES

Early antibiotic therapy alters or halts the typical progression.

Stage Gross Microscopic 1. Congestion Affected lobe heavy, red, boggy
Vascular congestion; proteinaceous fluid with scattered neutrophils and many bacteria in alveoli. Lasts a few days
2. Red hepatization Lobe has the consistency of a liver
Alveoli packed with neutrophils, RBCs and fibrin; pleura shows fibrinous or fibrinopurulent exudate
3. Grey hepatization Lung dry, grey, firm
RBCs lysed while fibrinous exudate persists in alveoli 4. Resolution
Return toward normal
Exudate enzymatically digested and resorbed or expectorated; basic alveolar structure intact. Pleural exudate may resolve or organize, leaving fibrous thickening or adhesions


BRONCHOPNEUMONIA (LOBULAR PNEUMONIA)

Definition: infection of the terminal bronchioles that extends into the surrounding alveoli, producing patchy consolidation.

 * Foci of inflammatory consolidation distributed through one or more lobes, most frequently bilateral and basal. Lesions grey, red to yellow.
 * Foci may become confluent and look like lobar pneumonia.
 * Areas adjacent to consolidation are edematous and hyperemic; areas far away are normal.
 * Pleural involvement is less common than in lobar pneumonia.
 * Histology: focal suppurative exudate filling the bronchi, bronchioles and adjacent alveolar spaces.


VIRAL AND MYCOPLASMAL PNEUMONIA (PRIMARY ATYPICAL PNEUMONIA)

Patchy inflammatory changes largely confined to the interstitial tissue, without alveolar exudate.

 * Etiology (interstitial pneumonitis): most commonly respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), influenza and parainfluenza viruses, coronaviruses.
 * Gross: patchy to massive consolidation of one or both lungs; lungs heavy and congested.
 * Histology: the hallmark is the interstitial nature of the inflammation:
   1. Interstitial inflammation: thickened alveolar walls (congestion, oedema, mononuclear infiltrate of lymphocytes, macrophages, some plasma cells).
   2. Necrotizing bronchiolitis: necrosis of bronchiolar epithelium, inspissated secretions, mononuclear infiltrate.
   3. Reactive changes: proliferating bronchiolar and alveolar lining cells may form multinucleate giant cells and syncytia.
   4. Alveolar changes: in severe cases oedema fluid, fibrin, scanty exudate, and hyaline membranes like those of respiratory distress syndrome.

title: Typical Bacterial Pathogens (Pneumococcus and Haemophilus)
content:
TYPICAL BACTERIAL PATHOGENS (PNEUMOCOCCUS AND HAEMOPHILUS)

Community-acquired acute bacterial pneumonia.


1. STREPTOCOCCUS PNEUMONIAE

The most common agent; about 23 serotypes account for over 90% of pneumococcal pneumonias. Often associated with hemorrhagic pneumonitis and empyema.

 * Morphology: Gram-positive, capsulated, elongated cocci in pairs (diplococci); non-motile, non-spore forming.
 * Culture: enriched media, 5-10% CO2 (capnophilic), 37°C; produces alpha-hemolytic colonies. Very fragile; contains the enzyme autolysin, so it dissolves in bile.
 * Biochemical: catalase negative; ferments inulin.
 * Antigenicity: by capsular polysaccharide, 90 serotypes.
 * Virulence factors
   * Cellular: capsule (anti-phagocytic); protein adhesin (initial colonization).
   * Extracellular: pneumolysin (destroys ciliated epithelial cells); secretory IgA protease.
 * Laboratory diagnosis (specimen: sputum):
   * Gram-stained smear is diagnostic; capsular polysaccharide antigen by latex agglutination.
   * Culture on blood agar: alpha hemolysis. To differentiate from S. viridans: pneumococcus is optochin sensitive, bile soluble, ferments inulin.
 * Prevention: capsular polysaccharide polyvalent vaccine, given to immunocompromised persons and after splenectomy.

Streptococcus pneumoniae in tissue [api/images/QRD1quEwrSJP/spneumoniae-in-tissue.png]

Alpha-hemolytic colonies on blood agar [api/images/4j9s8R79nMOC/spneumoniae-alpha-hemolytic-colonies.png]


2. HAEMOPHILUS INFLUENZAE

 * Morphology: Gram-negative small thin bacilli; non-motile, non-spore forming; non-capsulated strains are isolated from sputum.
 * Culture: facultative anaerobe, 5% CO2. Chocolate agar is the medium of choice because it needs growth factors from red cells: X (haem) and V (NAD).
 * Virulence factors: neuraminidase and IgA protease.
 * Disease: non-typable (non-capsulated) strains cause localized mucosal infection; they are the most common cause of chronic pulmonary infection in adults because most adults have natural antibody to the capsule.
 * Diagnosis: sputum Gram stain; culture directly on chocolate agar at 37°C with CO2; identified by Gram stain and latex agglutination.
 * Immunity: antibody to somatic (cell wall) antigens.

title: Chlamydia pneumoniae
content:
CHLAMYDIA PNEUMONIAE

اللقب: صاحب الالتهاب الرئوي غير النمطي، بلا مستودع حيواني


بطاقة الهوية | ID CARD

الحقل (Field) المعلومة (Information) الاسم العلمي (Scientific name)
Chlamydia pneumoniae النوع (Type)
طفيليات صغيرة إجبارية داخل الخلايا (obligate intracellular)؛ تحتوي DNA وRNA وريبوسومات وتصنع بروتيناتها، فهي بكتيريا حقيقية
الغشاء (Membrane)
غشاء داخلي وخارجي مثل سالبة الجرام (Gram-negative) مع lipopolysaccharide، بلا طبقة peptidoglycan
الصبغة (Staining) لا تتلون بجرام، وتتلون بـ Giemsa نقطة ضعف (Weak point)
تصنع أغلب وسائطها الاستقلابية لكنها لا تصنع ATP بنفسها الزرع
في كيس الصفار لجنين الدجاج أو في مزارع الأنسجة الشكلان (Two forms)
Elementary body (EB): صغير 0.3-0.4 ميكرومتر، الشكل المعدي، غشاؤه صلب ويقاوم الظروف السيئة، يرتبط بمستقبلات الخلية. Reticulate body (RB): غير معدٍ، داخل الخلية، نشط استقلابيا ويتكاثر، غشاؤه هش
دورة الحياة (Life cycle)
يلتصق EB بالخلية ويُبتلع (endocytosis أو phagocytosis) ← داخل الجسيم الداخلي (endosome) يتحول إلى RB ويمنع اندماج الـ endosome مع الليزوزومات فيقاوم القتل داخل الخلية ← RB يتكاثر بالانشطار الثنائي ← يعود إلى EB ← ثم تتحلل الخلية (C. psittaci) أو يُطرد الجسم المتضمّن بعكس الالتقام (C. pneumoniae)

Developmental cycle of Chlamydia [api/images/kjvui55u4vVF/micro-chlamydia-developmental-cycle.png]


السجل الجنائي | CRIMINAL RECORD

الحقل (Field) المعلومة (Information) التهمة (Charge / disease)
الالتهاب الرئوي غير النمطي (Walking pneumonia)
طريقة الدخول (Route of entry / transmission)
القطيرات التنفسية (respiratory droplets). لا يوجد مستودع حيواني
الأسلحة (Weapons / virulence factors)
بقاؤه داخل الـ endosome ومنع اندماجه بالليزوزومات
ارتباطات مريبة (Suspicious associations)
ارتباط عال بـ تصلب الشرايين وأمراض القلب ومرض ألزهايمر والربو عند البالغين
الضحايا المفضلون (Preferred victims / risk groups) غير مذكور في الملف
فترة الحضانة (Incubation period) غير مذكور في الملف
أعراض الجريمة (Crime signs / symptoms) غير مذكور في الملف
طريقة الكشف (التحقيق) (Detection / lab diagnosis)
مباشر: immunofluorescence وELISA لكشف المستضد (antigen)، وPCR. الزرع (culture): في مزرعة نسيجية مناسبة. مصليا: ارتفاع العيار أربعة أضعاف في عينتين متزامنتين بـ complement fixation أو ELISA يدل على العدوى، وارتفاع IgM يدل على عدوى حديثة

التتراسايكلين (tetracycline)ات، أزيثرومايسين، إريثروميسين، سلفوناميدات. ولا تُعطى التتراسايكلينات للمواليد لتجنب تلوّن الأسنان

السجل الجنائي | CRIMINAL RECORD

الحقل (Field) المعلومة (Information) التهمة (Charge / disease)
الالتهاب الرئوي (pneumonia) عند الرضع (infants) والأطفال (children) والبالغين، وعدوى مخاطية موضعية. وعند البالغين المصابين بمرض رئوي مزمن تكون السلالات غير المحفظية (non-typable) أكثر سبب للعدوى، لأن أغلب البالغين لديهم أجسام مضادة طبيعية ضد سكر المحفظة (capsule)
طريقة الدخول (Route of entry / transmission) غير مذكور في الملف
الأسلحة (Virulence factors) Neuraminidase وIgA protease
الضحايا المفضلون (Preferred victims / risk groups)
الرضع (infants) والأطفال (children) والبالغون؛ ومرضى الرئة المزمن. ويظهر أيضا كسبب لالتهاب رئوي (pneumonia) جرثومي بعد الإنفلونزا (influenza)
فترة الحضانة (Incubation period) غير مذكور في الملف
أعراض الجريمة (Crime signs / symptoms) غير مذكور في الملف
طريقة الكشف (التحقيق) (Detection / lab diagnosis)
العينة: البلغم (sputum). مسحة بصبغة جرام (Gram stain). زرع مباشر على chocolate agar عند 37°م مع CO2. التعرف على المستعمرات (colonies) بصبغة جرام، و latex agglutination، والتألق المناعي (immunofluorescence)، و DNA probes
المناعة (Immunity) أجسام مضادة ضد المستضد (antigen) الجسدي (جدار الخلية)
العقوبة (العلاج) (Punishment / treatment)
في العدوى الخطيرة: سيفالوسبورينات الجيل الثالث هي الدواء المفضل. وقد تظهر مقاومة (resistance) عند استعمال الأمبيسلين (ampicillin)
الوقاية (الحبس) (Prevention / containment)
تتكون أجسام مضادة IgG تمنح مناعة عند الأطفال (children). والتوصيات الحالية لتطعيم الرضع (infants) ابتداء من عمر شهرين: ثلاثة لقاح (vaccine)ات بالحقن هي DTP (الخناق والكزاز والسعال (cough) الديكي) وHib المقترن (يحمي الأطفال من النمط b) والتهاب الكبد B. (تضيف الشريحة عبارة غير واضحة: «It does not protect against diseases»)

 * أدوية (Drugs): Hib conjugate vaccine • Penicillins
 * أدوات تشخيص (Diagnostic tools): Direct fluorescent antibody / Immunofluorescence • Gram stain • Latex agglutination • PCR • Special culture media

title: Klebsiella pneumoniae
content:
KLEBSIELLA PNEUMONIAE (الكلبسيلا)

اللقب: صاحب الكبسولة المخاطية السميكة


بطاقة الهوية | ID CARD

الحقل (Field) المعلومة (Information) الاسم العلمي (Scientific name)
Klebsiella pneumoniae. أنواع الجنس: K. oxytoca وK. rhinoscleromatis وK. ozaenae
النوع (Type) بكتيريا سالبة الجرام (Gram-negative bacteria)
الشكل (Morphology / shape) عصيات (bacilli)، منفردة أو أزواجا أو سلاسل قصيرة
المحفظة / الحركة / الأبواغ (Capsule / motility / spores)
لها محفظة (هي عامل الضراوة وتصنع المستعمرات (colonies) المخاطية mucoid)، غير متحركة (non-motile) (لا مستضد (antigen) H)، لا تكوّن أبواغا (non-spore-forming)
التنفس والنمو (Respiration & growth)
هوائية ولاهوائية اختيارية (facultative anaerobe)؛ مستعمرات (colonies) كبيرة رطبة بسبب كبسولة السكر المتعدد المخاطية (K antigen)؛ تخمّر اللاكتوز على MacConkey
البصمة الكيميائية (Biochemical reactions)
تخمّر الجلوكوز واللاكتوز والمالتوز والمانيتول والسكروز والساليسين بإنتاج حمض وغاز. Indole سالب، methyl red سالب، VP موجب، citrate موجب (IMVC: --++)
الأنماط (Serotypes / types) 80 نمطا مصليا حسب السكر المتعدد للمحفظة
الموطن والأصل (Habitat & reservoir / origin)
الجهاز التنفسي والمعوي والبولي التناسلي عند الإنسان (human)، وفي التربة (soil) والماء (water)

Capsulated Klebsiella [api/images/5vp5bcx3jKq7/micro-klebsiella-capsules.png]


السجل الجنائي | CRIMINAL RECORD

الحقل (Field) المعلومة (Information) التهمة (Charge / disease)
التهاب رئوي مكتسب من المجتمع، وخاصة عند مرضى الرئة المزمن ومرضى السكري (diabetes mellitus)، ويُذكر أيضا بين عوامل الالتهاب الرئوي (pneumonia) المستشفوي. وسلالاتها المنتجة لـ ESBL تُعزل من بيئة المستشفى وتسبب عدوى خطيرة
طريقة الدخول (Route of entry / transmission)
المصدر ذاتي (endogenous) أو استنشاق قطيرات تنفسية (respiratory droplets)
الأسلحة (Weapons / virulence factors)
الكبسولة (تعيق البلع وتساعد الالتصاق)؛ السم الداخلي Endotoxin (حمى (fever) والتهاب وصدمة إنتانية)؛ إنزيمات: cephalosporinases وESBL المسؤولة عن مقاومة (resistance) السيفالوسبورينات (cephalosporins)
الضحايا المفضلون (Preferred victims / risk groups)
مرضى الرئة المزمن، مرضى السكري (diabetes mellitus)
فترة الحضانة (Incubation period) غير مذكور في الملف
أعراض الجريمة (Crime signs / symptoms) غير مذكور في الملف
طريقة الكشف (التحقيق) (Detection / lab diagnosis)
الزرع (culture) على MacConkey (مستعمرات (colonies) مخاطية، تخمّر اللاكتوز) والاختبارات الكيميائية. اختبار الحساسية للمضادات ضروري مع تحديد سلالات ESBL
العقوبة (العلاج) (Punishment / treatment)
K. pneumoniae مقاومة (resistance) طبيعيا للأمبيسلين (intrinsically resistant). والمقاومة المتزايدة تفرض فحص الحساسية دائما
الوقاية (Prevention) غير مذكور في الملف

ملفات القضية (Case files = lecture notes): Nosocomial Pathogens


روابط المصطلحات | LINKED TERMS

 * أعراض وعلامات (Symptoms & signs): Fever
 * أدوية (Drugs): Cephalosporins
 * أدوات تشخيص (Diagnostic tools): Bacterial identification tests • Special culture media

title: Legionella pneumophila
content:
LEGIONELLA PNEUMOPHILA (الفيلقية)

اللقب: ساكن مياه الأبراج والنوافير، لا ينتقل بين الأشخاص


بطاقة الهوية | ID CARD

الحقل (Field) المعلومة (Information) الاسم العلمي (Scientific name)
Legionella pneumophila النوع (Type)
بكتيريا سالبة الجرام (Gram-negative bacteria) الشكل (Morphology / shape)
عصيات (bacilli) صغيرة الحركة / الأبواغ (Motility / spores)
متحركة (motile)، لا تكوّن أبواغا (non-spore-forming) التنفس (Respiration) هوائية
وسط الزرع (Culture medium)
BCYE agar (buffered charcoal yeast extract). تحتاج السيستين فلا تنمو على آجار الدم (blood agar). الحضانة (incubation) 35-46°م لمدة 10 أيام، وتؤكد المستعمرات (colonies) بتقنيات مناعية
طريقة المعيشة (Lifestyle)
ممرضة داخل الخلايا اختياريا (facultative intracellular)، تنمو داخل العدلات (neutrophils) والبلعميات (macrophages) الرئوية
الموطن والأصل (Habitat & reservoir / origin)
منتشرة في بيئات كثيرة وخاصة مصادر المياه؛ تتكاثر داخل الأوالي والأميبات. المصدر: أنظمة الماء (water) الساخن المنزلية، النوافير، أبراج التبريد

Cellular pathogenesis of Legionella [api/images/4JOwjR8z3zq4/micro-legionella-pathogenesis.png]


السجل الجنائي | CRIMINAL RECORD

الحقل (Field) المعلومة (Information) التهمة (Charge / disease)
مرض الفيلق (Legionnaires' disease) وهو التهاب رئوي. وهي أيضا من العوامل المعزولة كثيرا في الالتهاب الرئوي (pneumonia) المستشفوي
طريقة الدخول (Route of entry / transmission)
قطيرات تحتوي البكتيريا. لم يثبت انتقالها من شخص لآخر، والمرض غير معدٍ ولا تلزم احتياطات خاصة
الأسلحة (Weapons / virulence factors)
تنمو داخل العدلات (neutrophils) والبلعميات (macrophages)، وكثيرا ما تهرب من المناعة الخلوية (cell-mediated immunity) التي هي الدفاع الرئيسي ضدها. (في الشكل: الجسيم البلعمي لا يتحمض ولا يندمج مع الليزوزوم، ثم تتكاثر داخله وتتمزق الخلية وتهرب البكتيريا)
الضحايا المفضلون (Preferred victims / risk groups)
ضعف المناعة (immunosuppression)، التدخين (smoking)، سرطان الرئة (lung cancer)، الفشل الكلوي (renal failure)
فترة الحضانة (Incubation period) نحو أسبوعين
أعراض الجريمة (Crime signs / symptoms)
تبدأ بأعراض (symptoms) تشبه الإنفلونزا (influenza): حمى، قشعريرة (chills)، سعال جاف. وفي المراحل المتقدمة: إسهال (diarrhea)، غثيان (nausea)، والتهاب رئوي (pneumonia)
طريقة الكشف (التحقيق) (Detection / lab diagnosis)
أربع طرق رئيسية: (أ) DFA وPCR، (ب) العزل (isolation) على الأوساط، (ج) الفحص المصلي بقياس الأجسام المضادة (antibodies)، (د) كشف المستضد في البول (antigenuria). وللكشف السريع في عينة الماء (water): PCR وDFA
العقوبة (العلاج) (Punishment / treatment)
أقوى مضادين: الماكروليدات (macrolides) (أزيثرومايسين) والكينولونات (quinolones) (سيبروفلوكساسين) لأنها تدخل الخلايا وتقتل البكتيريا
الوقاية (Prevention) غير مذكور في الملف

ملفات القضية (Case files = lecture notes): Atypical Pathogens


روابط المصطلحات | LINKED TERMS

 * أدوية (Drugs): Fluoroquinolones • Macrolides
 * أدوات تشخيص (Diagnostic tools): Direct fluorescent antibody / Immunofluorescence • PCR • Special culture media • Urinary antigen test

title: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
content:
MYCOBACTERIUM TUBERCULOSIS (عصية السل)

اللقب: المجرم البطيء الصبور، يختبئ داخل البلعميات سنوات


بطاقة الهوية | ID CARD

الحقل (Field) المعلومة (Information) الاسم العلمي (Scientific name)
Mycobacterium tuberculosis النوع (Type)
بكتيريا عصوية مقاومة (resistance) للحمض والكحول (acid-alcohol fast)
اكتشافها (Discovery) زرعها روبرت كوخ عام 1882 الشكل (Morphology / shape)
عصيات (bacilli) رفيعة منحنية قليلا. بصبغة Ziehl-Neelsen تظهر حبالا حمراء متعرجة على خلفية زرقاء
المحفظة / الحركة / الأبواغ (Capsule / motility / spores)
غير محفظية، غير متحركة (non-motile)، لا تكوّن أبواغا (non-spore-forming)
التنفس والنمو (Respiration & growth)
هوائية إجبارية (obligate aerobe) عند 37°م، ويحسّن النمو ثاني أكسيد الكربون 5-10%
سرعة النمو (Growth rate)
بطيئة: زمن التضاعف 18-24 ساعة؛ العزل (isolation) الأولي للمستعمرات (colonies) من 2 إلى 8 أسابيع
الجدار (سر قوتها) (Cell wall / source of strength)
جدار سميك معقد غني بالدهون الشمعية خارج الببتيدوغليكان. الدهون 60% من الجدار: mycolic acid، phosphatides، cord factor، waxes، sulfatides. هذا يفسر عدم تلونها بجرام، وبقاءها داخل البلعميات (macrophages)، ومقاومتها لتحلل المتمم، ومقاومتها لكثير من المضادات والأحماض والقلويات
مقاومة للـ (Resistant to)
الجفاف (خاصة في البلغم (sputum))، الأحماض (3% HCl و6% H2SO4) والقلويات (4% NaOH)، الأصباغ (malachite green)، بعض المضادات (البنسلين (penicillin))، الظلام
حساسة للـ (Sensitive to)
الحرارة الرطبة (60°م 30 دقيقة، أو 70°م 3 دقائق ثم تبريد مفاجئ، أي البسترة)، المطهرات (glutaraldehyde والكحول)، الأدوية (ريفامبين، PAS، ستربتومايسين، أيزونيازيد، بيرازيناميد)، الأشعة فوق البنفسجية وضوء الشمس
الحيوانات الحساسة (Susceptible animals)
خنزير غينيا يتأثر بـ M. tuberculosis و M. bovis بنفس القدر؛ الأرنب يتأثر بـ M. bovis فقط

Ziehl-Neelsen stain of M. tuberculosis [api/images/o4DGr6wNy3Ga/micro-mtb-ziehl-neelsen.png]

Lowenstein-Jensen medium [api/images/wiXPxW4CST07/micro-mtb-lj-medium.png]

M. tuberculosis colonies on L-J medium [api/images/w8Vq7ej6BUNm/micro-mtb-colonies-lj.png]

Schematic diagram of the mycobacterial wall [api/images/T0JuKTERLrNh/micro-mtb-cell-wall.png]

Primary versus post-primary tuberculosis [api/images/zFvpjhny6seq/micro-tb-primary-vs-postprimary.png]

Tuberculin test (Mantoux) [api/images/AXQuOVSashiQ/micro-tuberculin-test.png]


السجل الجنائي | CRIMINAL RECORD

الحقل (Field) المعلومة (Information) التهمة (Charge / disease)
السل (Tuberculosis): مرض مزمن تتكون فيه حبيبة التهابية موضعية (granuloma). العدوى التنفسية تمثل 85% من الحالات، لكنه يصيب أي عضو. السل الدخني (Miliary) عند انتشار بؤر صغيرة في أغلب أعضاء الجسم. وتزداد حالات السلالات المقاومة (resistance) لعدة أدوية
طريقة الدخول (Route of entry / transmission)
1) محمول جوا: استنشاق قطيرات أقل من 5 ميكرومتر تصل إلى الحويصلات. 2) ابتلاع حليب ملوث بـ M. bovis (أو M. tuberculosis بالخطأ) فتحدث عدوى معوية. 3) تلقيح مباشر عبر خدش في الجلد
الأسلحة (Virulence factors)
لا يفرز سموما خارجية ولا يحمل سما داخليا. يفضّل البلعميات (macrophages) والخلايا الشبكية البطانية حيث يعيش ويتكاثر. أسلحته في الجدار: mycolic acid مع peptidoglycan (يحفز تكوّن الحبيبة)؛ Phosphatide (يحفز تكاثر الوحيدات والتجبن)؛ Cord factor (سم خلوي يمنع هجرة الكريات البيضاء ويكوّن حبيبة مزمنة)؛ Wax D (مساعد مناعي adjuvant)؛ Sulfatides (تمنع اندماج الجسيم البلعمي مع الليزوزوم فيبقى حيا داخل البلعم)؛ البروتينات (تسبب حساسية السلين من النوع IV)؛ السكري (diabetes mellitus)ات (دورها غير مؤكد وتحرض فرط الحساسية (hypersensitivity))
الضحايا المفضلون (Preferred victims / risk groups)
مدمنو المخدرات بالحقن، ومرضى HIV فترة الحضانة (Incubation period)
غير مذكورة. لكن المناعة الخلوية (cell-mediated immunity) تبدأ بعد 2-10 أسابيع من العدوى
مراحل الجريمة (Stages of the crime / pathogenesis)
آفات نضحية (exudative): التهاب حاد في الرئة، وبعد أسبوعين تصل العصيات (bacilli) للعقد اللمفية فتتضخم. آفة حبيبية: بعد 2-10 أسابيع تتكون الحبيبة (tubercle) ويتجبن مركزها (caseation necrosis). ثم قد تنفتح الدرنة في قصبة وتكوّن تجويفا، أو تشفى بالتليف أو التكلس. Ghon complex: الآفة الأولية في الرئة مع العقد المتضخمة
السل الأولي والثانوي (Primary vs post-primary TB)
الأولي: آفة واحدة في الفص الأوسط أو السفلي الأيمن مع تضخم العقد الصارفة. ما بعد الأولي: من إعادة تنشيط عدوى كامنة أو عدوى جديدة؛ آفة واحدة متجوفة في قمة الرئة، بلا تضخم عقد، وفرط الحساسية (hypersensitivity) المتأخر (DHR) يسرّع التجبن
كامن أم نشط (Latent vs active)
كامن (Latent): 90% ممن لديهم اختبار سلين إيجابي، بلا أعراض (symptoms)، العصيات (bacilli) خاملة، البلغم (sputum) سلبي، لا ينقل العدوى. المرض (Disease): 10%، يتغلب فيه الميكروب على المناعة، البلغم إيجابي، ينقل العدوى
أعراض الجريمة (Crime signs / symptoms)
أعراض (symptoms) غير نوعية: توعك، إرهاق، تعرق ليلي، حمى (fever) خفيفة، نقص وزن. وفي العدوى التنفسية: سعال (cough) مستمر وبصاق دم (haemoptysis)
طريقة الكشف (التحقيق) (Detection / lab diagnosis)
العينات: 3 عينات بلغم متتالية صباحية، غسيل قصبي سنخي (bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL)) أو خزعة رئة، وللأطفال أو من لا يستطيع إخراج البلغم (sputum): سحب المعدة. التحضير: تمييع بـ N-acetyl-L-cysteine، تطهير بـ NaOH، تعديل ثم تركيز بالتثفيل. المجهر (microscopy): صبغة ZN (عصيات (bacilli) وردية منحنية على خلفية زرقاء). الزرع (التشخيص القاطع): حتى 8 أسابيع، وBactec/MGIT خلال 6-12 يوما. PCR: تشخيص سريع خلال 1-2 يوم لكنه لا يغني عن الزرع واختبار الحساسية. اختبارات مناعية: اختبار السلين (Mantoux)، QuantiFERON/IGRA، ALS، واللاصقة الجلدية
العقوبة (العلاج) (Punishment / treatment)
أدوية مضادة للسل مجتمعة لمدة 6 أشهر على الأقل؛ العلاج المركب يمنع نشوء المقاومة (resistance) بسبب طول المدة. وتوصي منظمة الصحة العالمية بـ DOTS (العلاج القصير تحت الإشراف المباشر)
الوقاية (الحبس) (Prevention / containment)
علاج المرضى النشطين، القضاء على السل في الماشية وبسترة الحليب، احتياطات الهواء في المستشفيات. علاج وقائي بالأيزونيازيد (isoniazid) 6-9 أشهر للأطفال ومن يتلقون كبت المناعة ومن تحوّل اختبار السلين لديهم إلى إيجابي. لقاح (vaccine) BCG: حي مضعف من M. bovis، يُعطى في الأدمة للمواليد أو لسلبيي اختبار السلين شديدي التعرض كالعاملين الصحيين، فوق العضلة الدالية. مناعته محدودة المدة وهو موضع جدل

ملفات القضية (Case files = lecture notes): Pulmonary Tuberculosis | Epidemiology and Microbiology | Pathogenesis | Laboratory Diagnosis | Management and Prevention | Anti-TB Drugs


روابط المصطلحات | LINKED TERMS

 * أعراض وعلامات (Symptoms & signs): Cough • Fever • Hemoptysis • Sputum
 * أدوية (Drugs): BCG vaccine • Isoniazid • Mucolytics • Penicillins • Second-line anti-TB drugs
 * أدوات تشخيص (Diagnostic tools): Bronchoalveolar lavage • IGRA / QuantiFERON-Gold • PCR • Tuberculin skin test • Ziehl-Neelsen

title: Mycoplasma pneumoniae
content:
MYCOPLASMA PNEUMONIAE

اللقب: صاحب الالتهاب الرئوي الماشي، بلا جدار خلوي


بطاقة الهوية | ID CARD

الحقل (Field) المعلومة (Information) الاسم العلمي (Scientific name)
Mycoplasma pneumoniae النوع (Type) بكتيريا بلا جدار خلوي
الشكل (Morphology / shape) متعددة الأشكال (pleomorphic) الصبغة (Staining)
لا تتلون بجرام، وتتلون بصبغة Giemsa الغشاء (Membrane)
غشاء خلوي فقط (لا peptidoglycan)، فيه sterols لكنها لا تصنّع الكوليسترول
الحجم (Size) صغيرة 0.2-0.8 ميكرومتر، تمر عبر مرشحات البكتيريا
الاستقلاب (Metabolism)
تفتقر إلى كثير من المسارات الاستقلابية، وتنمو في أجنة الدجاج
التنفس (Respiration) هوائي إجباري (strict aerobe)
الموطن والأصل (Habitat & reservoir / origin) مستودعها الجهاز التنفسي البشري

Mycoplasma fried-egg colonies [api/images/Yl9fpL8FNFOg/micro-mycoplasma-fried-egg-colonies.png]

Chest X-ray in Mycoplasma pneumonia [api/images/c6bqwoWO8pWs/micro-mycoplasma-chest-xray.png]


السجل الجنائي | CRIMINAL RECORD

الحقل (Field) المعلومة (Information) التهمة (Charge / disease)
السبب الأكثر شيوعا للالتهاب الرئوي غير النمطي الأولي، ويسمى Walking pneumonia
طريقة الدخول (Route of entry / transmission) القطيرات
الأسلحة (Weapons / virulence factors)
بروتين Cytoadhesin (P1) يمكّنها من تثبيط حركة أهداب القصبات. وغياب الجدار يجعلها لا تتأثر بالبنسلين (penicillin) وبقية مضادات β-lactam
الضحايا المفضلون (Preferred victims / risk groups) الأعمار الصغيرة (5-15 سنة)
فترة الحضانة (Incubation period) 2-3 أسابيع
أعراض الجريمة (Crime signs / symptoms)
حمى (fever)، صداع (headache)، سعال (cough) غير منتج
طريقة الكشف (التحقيق) (Detection / lab diagnosis)
في البداية يعتمد التشخيص على السريريات. مباشر: direct fluorescent antibody وPCR. الزرع (culture): بلغم أو غسيل حلق في وسط نقل خاص؛ تظهر مستعمرات (colonies) «البيضة المقلية» على آجار مدعم بالمصل بعد 3 أسابيع؛ وتعرف بالتألق المناعي وPCR. مصليا: Complement fixation (لا تبلغ الذروة قبل 4-6 أسابيع، وارتفاع أربعة أضعاف يدل على عدوى حديثة)، وELISA لكشف IgM. غير نوعي: Cold agglutinins، أجسام IgM تلصق كريات الدم الحمراء من الزمرة O عند 4°م لا عند 37°م؛ عيارها 125 فأكثر يدل على عدوى حديثة
العقوبة (العلاج) (Punishment / treatment)
التتراسايكلين (للبالغين فقط)، الإريثروميسين (erythromycin)، والكينولونات (quinolones)
الوقاية (Prevention) غير مذكور في الملف

روابط المصطلحات | LINKED TERMS

 * أعراض وعلامات (Symptoms & signs): Cough • Fever
 * أدوية (Drugs): Fluoroquinolones • Macrolides • Penicillins
 * أدوات تشخيص (Diagnostic tools): Cold agglutinins • Direct fluorescent antibody / Immunofluorescence • PCR • Serology
